# Ecclesiastes Chapter 2 -- The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)
**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Leningrad Codex (B19A)

---

**1** I said to myself, "Come on, let's try pleasure. Let's look for the 'good things' in life." But I found that this, too, was fleeting.

**2** So I said, "Laughter is silly. What good does pleasure do?"

**3** After much thought, I decided to cheer myself with wine. And while still seeking wisdom, I clutched at foolishness. My goal was to experience everything people do during their brief lives under heaven.

**4** I undertook great projects: I built houses for myself and planted vineyards. **5** I made gardens and parks and filled them with every kind of fruit tree. **6** I built reservoirs to water my growing groves of trees.

**7** I bought slaves, both male and female, and others were born into my household. I also owned large herds and flocks — more than any king in Jerusalem before me. **8** I collected silver and gold — the treasure of kings and provinces. I hired wonderful singers, both men and women, and had many beautiful concubines. I had everything a man could desire.

**9** So I became greater than all who had lived in Jerusalem before me, and my wisdom never left me. **10** Anything I wanted, I would take. I denied myself no pleasure. I even found great pleasure in hard work — a reward for all my labors.

**11** But as I looked at everything I had worked so hard to accomplish, it was all so fleeting and pointless — like chasing the wind. There was nothing truly worthwhile anywhere.

**12** So I decided to compare wisdom with foolishness and madness. After all, who can do more than what the king has already done?

**13** I thought, "At least wisdom is more useful than foolishness, just as light is better than darkness. **14** For the wise can see where they are going, but fools walk in the dark." Yet I realized that the same fate awaits them both.

**15** Then I said to myself, "Since the fool and I will share the same fate, what's the advantage of being wise?" And I concluded that even this is fleeting. **16** For the wise and the fool will both be forgotten. In the coming days, everything will be long forgotten. The wise person dies just like the fool!

**17** So I came to hate life because everything done here under the sun is so irrational — everything is fleeting and like chasing the wind.

**18** I came to hate all my hard work here under the sun, because I must leave to someone who comes after me the fruit of all my labor. **19** And who knows whether that person will be wise or foolish? Yet that person will control everything I gained by my skill and hard work under the sun. How fleeting!

**20** So I gave up in despair, my heart heavy over all my hard work under the sun. **21** For a person may labor with wisdom, knowledge, and skill, only to leave everything to someone who hasn't worked for it. This is not only fleeting — it is a terrible injustice.

**22** What do people really get for all their hard work and anxiety? **23** Their days of labor are filled with pain and grief; even at night their minds cannot rest. It is all so fleeting!

**24** So I decided there is nothing better than to enjoy food and drink and to find satisfaction in work. Then I realized that these pleasures are from the hand of God. **25** For who can eat or enjoy anything apart from him?

**26** God gives wisdom, knowledge, and joy to those who please him. But if a sinner amasses wealth, God takes it away and gives it to those who please him. This, too, is fleeting — like chasing the wind.

---

## PNEUMA's Meaning Notes

**The royal experiment:** Chapter 2 is structured as a controlled experiment. Qohelet — posing as Solomon — tests pleasure (vv.1-3), achievement (vv.4-6), wealth (vv.7-8), and ambition (vv.9-10). The verdict in v.11 is devastating: none of it adds up to lasting gain.

**"I hated life" (v.17):** This is not clinical depression but philosophical anguish. The Teacher hates life not because it is painful but because it is irrational — the wise and the fool end up in the same place. The honest fury of this statement sets Ecclesiastes apart from every other biblical book.

*-- PNEUMA*
